newsitem.title: MEXICO: Final result seen showing historic change in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Final result seen showing historic change in Mexico.

text.p: Final results from Mexico's mid-term elections due out on Wednesday were expected to show the country's ruling party had suffered its worst setback in seven decades.

Although the Institutional Revolutionary Party's (PRI) loss in a landmark Mexico City race was certain, a final count was seen clearing up lingering doubts as to whether the PRI also lost its grip on Congress for the first time.

A definitive tally could also spark the first serious protest of the election from an opposition which made historic gains during the vote but has said it was still cheated of victory in some state and local races.

Early voting results showed President Ernesto Zedillo's PRI, which has ruled Mexico since 1929, badly beaten in the first-ever Mexico City mayor race by outspoken PRI critic and leftist veteran Cuauhtemoc Cardenas.
But things were not so clear in the lower house of Congress, which up to now simply rubber-stamped most presidential initiatives.

Of 300 directly elected seats in the lower house, the PRI had 161 against 71 for Cardenas' Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and 67 for the conservative National Action Party (PAN), with some 87 percent of votes counted.

The remaining 200 seats will be allocated by proportional representation according to each party's share of the overall vote. With 86 percent of the vote counted, the PRI had won about 39 percent, the PAN 27 percent and the PRD 25.5 percent.
While most analysts agree the PRI will likely fall about 10 seats short of a majority in the 500-seat body, the extent of its loss could play a major role in passing future legislation, they said.
Mexico's newly independent Federal Electoral Institute (IFE) said on Tuesday it planned to start the final count early on Wednesday and issue full results late in the day.

Although the poll was seen as Mexico's cleanest to date overall, opposition parties on Tuesday began to cast doubt over some of the individual races -- especially in two hotly contested gubernatorial contests.
The PAN said it refused to accept a preliminary result in the northern state of Sonora showing PRI candidate Armando Lopez Nogales winning the governorship over the PAN's Enrique Salgado.

"It is impossible to accept, that in a state where the opposition governs 84 percent of the municipalities, the PRI claims it won the gubernatorial race ... Besides, the PRI lost its majority in the state congress and lost every race for federal congress, according to the results," Salgado said.

And in the impoverished southern state of Campeche, some 12,000 people led by PRD state candidate Layda Sansores took to the streets of the state capital to protest alleged fraud by the PRI, chanting "We're with you Layda," "We want no more fraud," and "Campechans unite."

On a national level, however, things were quiet, almost friendly between opposing political forces. Even before final results, Zedillo began courting the opposition to prevent legislative gridlock when Congress opens in September.

In an unusual gesture, he held out the hand of friendship to main opposition parties that he had tirelessly attacked during the election campaign, and paid special tribute to an unlikely bedfellow -- the leftist PRD.
